questions.question: In the programming part of Stochastic Operations Research, which description of a closure is correct?
options: A function that calls itself on smaller inputs until it reaches a base case it can answer directly.
An anonymous function written where it is used, such as $x\mapsto x^2$, without being given a name.
An inner function returned by an outer function that keeps the outer call's variables after that call ends.
A dictionary that stores each computed result under its argument, so repeated calls become lookups.

questions.question: Let $\operatorname{power}(e)$ return $b\mapsto b^{e}$. What kind of object is $\operatorname{power}(2)$?
options: The function $b\mapsto b^{2}$, in which the exponent $e=2$ is fixed.
The number $2^{2}=4$, obtained by using $2$ as base and exponent.
The function $e\mapsto 2^{e}$, in which the base $2$ is fixed.
An error, because no value of $b$ has been supplied yet.

questions.question: Let $\operatorname{power}(e)$ return $b\mapsto b^{e}$. What does it mean to specialise this template to a cube function?
options: Edit the body of $\operatorname{power}$ so that the number $3$ replaces $e$, giving a second routine.
Write $\mathit{cube}=\operatorname{power}(3)(b)$, which gives the cube of one particular value $b$.
Rename the outer function as $\mathit{cube}$, so that $\mathit{cube}(e)$ returns $b\mapsto b^{e}$.
Call $\operatorname{power}(3)$ and name the returned function $\mathit{cube}$, so $\mathit{cube}(b)=b^{3}$.

questions.question: A pmf $p_X$ is stored as a map created by $\operatorname{Map}(\mathit{default}=0)$, which returns and stores the default value for a key seen for the first time. Why is $0$ the right default?
options: Zero is the neutral start value of a sum, which the map needs before it adds up the probabilities.
Values outside the support have probability zero, so reading such a value returns the correct $p_X(x)$.
With default zero a read of an unseen key leaves the map unchanged, so its keys remain the support.
With default zero the stored values sum to one whatever probabilities are stored under the keys.

questions.question: $\operatorname{CDF}(p_X)$ returns a closure $F$ with $F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x)$ for the pmf $p_X$. Which work is done once, in the outer call, rather than at every evaluation $F(x)$?
options: Finding the largest index $k$ with $s_k\leq x$ by search sorted, for the value $x$ that is queried.
Nothing: $F$ retains only $p_X$ and sorts and sums the probabilities again each time it is called.
Sorting the support into $s_1<\cdots<s_n$ and computing the cumulative sums $F_X(s_k)$.
Computing $F(x)$ for every real number $x$ and storing all of these values in a table.

questions.question: Let $\operatorname{power}(e)$ return $b\mapsto b^{e}$, $\operatorname{square}=\operatorname{power}(2)$ and $\operatorname{cube}=\operatorname{power}(3)$. What is $\operatorname{square}(5)+\operatorname{cube}(2)$?

Let $\operatorname{Exceeds}(b)$ return the function $w\mapsto\mathbf{1}\{w>b\}$, and put $\mathit{late}=\operatorname{Exceeds}(6)$. Five customers have waiting times $2,6,6,7,10$. What is $\mathit{late}(2)+\mathit{late}(6)+\mathit{late}(6)+\mathit{late}(7)+\mathit{late}(10)$?

A counter is created by $\mathit{counter}\gets\operatorname{Map}(\mathit{default}=0)$, and for the data $x=[2,5,2,2,7,5]$ the update $\mathit{counter}(x_k)\gets\mathit{counter}(x_k)+1$ is run for $k=1,\ldots,6$. How many keys does $\mathit{counter}$ hold, and what is $\mathit{counter}(2)$?
options: $3$ keys, and $\mathit{counter}(2)=3$
$6$ keys, and $\mathit{counter}(2)=3$
$3$ keys, and $\mathit{counter}(2)=1$
$3$ keys, and $\mathit{counter}(2)=2$

questions.question: For the pmf $p(2)=0.3$, $p(6)=0.7$, the closure $F=\operatorname{CDF}(p)$ finds the largest $k$ with $s_k\leq x$ and returns $F_X(s_k)$, or $0$ if $x<s_1$. What are $F(1.5)$ and $F(4)$?

A map is created by $M\gets\operatorname{Map}(\mathit{default}=0)$, which stores and returns the default for a key seen for the first time. After $M(1)\gets3$, the value $M(8)$ is read once. Which keys does $M$ hold?
options: Only the key $1$
The keys $1$ and $8$
The keys $1$ and $3$
The keys $1$, $3$ and $8$

questions.question: Let $\operatorname{power}(e)$ return $b\mapsto b^{e}$ and $\operatorname{square}=\operatorname{power}(2)$. Elsewhere in the program a different variable named $e$ is set to $10$. Which statement about $\operatorname{square}(3)$ is correct?
options: It equals $9$, because $\operatorname{square}$ uses the value $e=2$ of the call that created it.
It equals $3^{10}$, because the closure uses the value that a variable named $e$ has most recently.
It raises an error, because the call $\operatorname{power}(2)$ has finished and its $e$ no longer exists.
It equals $2^{3}=8$, because the retained value $2$ is the base and $3$ is the exponent.

questions.question: The scope of a variable is the part of a program in which it can be used. With $\operatorname{power}(e)$ returning $b\mapsto b^{e}$ and $\operatorname{square}=\operatorname{power}(2)$, which statement about the variable $e=2$ is correct?
options: After the call it can be used anywhere in the program, which is how $\operatorname{square}$ finds it.
It is removed when $\operatorname{power}$ returns, so $\operatorname{square}$ must be given $e$ again at each call.
It belongs to the whole routine $\operatorname{power}$, so a later call $\operatorname{power}(3)$ changes it to $3$.
It lives in the scope of the call $\operatorname{power}(2)$; outside code cannot use it, but $\operatorname{square}$ still can.

questions.question: $\operatorname{CDF}(p_X)$ returns a closure $F$ with $F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x)$. How does the function $F$ depend on the pmf $p_X$ and on the number $x$?
options: Both $p_X$ and $x$ are passed to $F$ at every call, so one $F$ serves all random variables.
The pmf $p_X$ is fixed when $F$ is created; each call of $F$ supplies only the argument $x$.
Only $x$ matters to $F$, so $\operatorname{CDF}(p)$ and $\operatorname{CDF}(q)$ return the same function.
The number $x$ is fixed when $F$ is created; each call of $F$ supplies a pmf $p_X$.

questions.question: Let $\operatorname{subtract}(b)$ return the function $a\mapsto a-b$. Put $g=\operatorname{subtract}(4)$ and $h=\operatorname{subtract}(g(10))$. What is $h(1)$?

Let $\operatorname{Exceeds}(b)$ return $w\mapsto\mathbf{1}\{w>b\}$, and let $\operatorname{Expectation}(p_X,f)=\sum_x f(x)\,p_X(x)$. For $p_X(1)=0.1$, $p_X(2)=0.2$, $p_X(3)=0.3$, $p_X(4)=0.4$, what is $\operatorname{Expectation}(p_X,\operatorname{Exceeds}(2))$?

For the pmf on $s=[1,2,4,7]$ with probabilities $0.1,0.4,0.3,0.2$, the closure $F=\operatorname{CDF}(p)$ finds the largest $k$ with $s_k\leq x$ and returns $F_X(s_k)$. Which index $k$ and value $F(4)$ result?

$\operatorname{Cache}()$ creates an empty dictionary $\mathit{cache}$ and returns it with the closure $\operatorname{InCache?}=q\mapsto(q\in\operatorname{keys}(\mathit{cache}))$. A memoised recursion stores its values in the dictionary from a first call of $\operatorname{Cache}()$ but, by mistake, tests membership with the $\operatorname{InCache?}$ from a second call. What goes wrong?
options: The test would see the same dictionary anyway, since both calls run the same code of $\operatorname{Cache}$.
The test would read a fresh empty dictionary, always answer false, and the cache would never save work.
The test would return stale values, so the memoised recursion would produce wrong results.
The test would fail, because a closure can only read a dictionary passed to it as an argument.

questions.question: The closure $F=\operatorname{CDF}(p)$ is created for a pmf map $p$, retaining the sorted support and cumulative sums computed in the outer call. Afterwards the stored probabilities in $p$ are changed. What does $F(x)$ return?
options: The cdf of the changed pmf, because a closure keeps access to the outer call's variables, including $p$.
An error for every $x$, because the retained support no longer matches the keys stored in $p$.
The changed cdf for $x$ at or above the first changed support point, and the old cdf below it.
The cdf of the pmf at the time of creation, because the sums were computed once in the outer call.

questions.question: A pmf is stored as $p\gets\operatorname{Map}(\mathit{default}=0)$, which stores and returns the default for a key seen for the first time; $p(1)\gets0.5$ and $p(3)\gets0.5$. The program reads $p(2)$ once and only then builds $F=\operatorname{CDF}(p)$, which takes the keys of $p$ as the support, sorts them and retains the cumulative sums $F_X(s_k)$. Which list of cumulative sums does $F$ retain?

$\operatorname{Cache}()$ creates an empty dictionary and returns it with a test $q\mapsto(q\in\operatorname{keys}(\cdot))$ for that dictionary. Put $(c_1,t_1)=\operatorname{Cache}()$, then $(c_2,t_2)=\operatorname{Cache}()$, store $c_1(4)\gets3$ and $c_2(7)\gets1$. What are $t_1(4)$, $t_1(7)$ and $t_2(4)$?
options: true, true, true
false, false, false
true, false, false
false, true, false
